sections.title: Cap and colour
sections.text: Tricholoma sulphureum (Bull.) P. Kumm., the sulphur knight, is a small to medium-sized agaric. Its cap is about 3–8 cm wide, convex at first then flattening, sometimes with a low central boss. The dry surface is sulphur-yellow, sometimes tinged olive, reddish brown or brown at the centre. The cap, gills, stem and flesh are yellow to sulphur-yellow.

sections.title: Gills, stem and smell
sections.text: The gills are thick and sulphur-yellow, adnate or notched near the stem; their spacing varies within the taxonomic complex. The yellow stem is about 2–7 cm long, sometimes longer in some accounts, and often has a whitish, slightly downy base; it has no ring or volva. The yellow flesh is thin and changes little when cut. The penetrating smell is often compared with coal gas or tar; its intensity and description vary. The spore print is white.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal species grows on the ground in broadleaf woods and parks, often with beech or oak. Several field sources report fruiting from summer into autumn, but timing varies by region.

sections.title: Look-alikes, taxonomy and toxicity
sections.text: Yellow colour and odour characterize sulphur knight in the broad sense, but other yellow or strong-smelling Tricholoma species exist and cannot always be separated from a photograph. A northern European molecular study distinguishes at least three cryptic lineages attributed to T. sulphureum; without a modern type, it is unknown which corresponds to the name in the strict sense. Tricholoma equestre is generally stockier, often with a viscid cap and more crowded gills, but this comparison does not confirm an identification. DGfM lists T. sulphureum among mushrooms associated with a gastrointestinal syndrome. Do not eat it; a page and an odour cannot securely identify a mushroom.

traits: Sulphur-yellow cap, 3–8 cm, convex then expanded, sometimes olive or brown-shaded at the centre
Thick sulphur-yellow gills, adnate to notched; spacing varies within the complex
Yellow stem, sometimes whitish and downy at the base; no ring or volva
Thin yellow flesh, white spore print; penetrating smell often compared with coal gas
Ectomycorrhizal in broadleaf woods, often with beech or oak; mainly summer to autumn
safetyNote: DGfM lists Tricholoma sulphureum among species associated with a gastrointestinal syndrome. Do not eat it. A smell, photograph or this entry is not enough to identify a specimen securely; contact a poison centre or emergency services if symptoms occur after ingestion.
